Gucci Fall 2026

Demna's Debut. Milan's Loudest Hour.

The Runway Reaction Index measures the 48-hour social, media, and search impact of a single fashion show. Gucci's Fall 2026 debut — Demna Gvasalia's first runway collection for the house — became the most-discussed show of Milan Fashion Week FW26 in a single hour. Here is the data behind the moment.

The Numbers

The Show

Nearly a year after Demna Gvasalia was hired to remake Gucci following his decade-long run at Balenciaga, he made his runway debut at the Palazzo Delle Scintille in Milan. The collection — titled "Primavera" after Sandro Botticelli's painting — was a declaration of intent: 83 looks spanning body-conscious minidresses, fluid tailored suits, and evening gowns, all threaded with the sexuality and cultural ambition that Demna believes defines the Gucci brand.

"My idea was to put Gucci back in the cultural spotlight," Demna told press after the show. The set — a museum-like hall lined with simulacra of Roman statuary, scanned and reproduced with the Uffizi's permission — made the statement architectural. Closing looks by Kate Moss and Karlie Kloss signaled the house's intention to reclaim its position at the apex of luxury fashion.

The Reaction

The Gucci show on February 27 at 2 PM generated 1.77 million social media mentions in a single hour — the highest single-show peak recorded across all of Milan Fashion Week FW26, according to Onclusive's social listening platform, which tracked 153 brands and 173 ambassadors across X, Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, and Threads.

Sentiment was mixed but predominantly positive. Fashion critics praised the emotional range of the collection and its cultural ambition. Social media users were more divided — some calling it "ridiculous," others declaring it "glamorous, sexy, dramatic and very intentional." The polarization itself drove engagement: controversy is an amplifier.

Share of Voice — MFW FW26

Among 153 fashion brands tracked during Milan Fashion Week FW26, Gucci ranked second in overall share of voice with 18.82% — just 0.29 percentage points behind Tod's, whose Thai celebrity ambassador strategy dominated early-week conversation. The tightest race of the season.

Media Impact Value

Launchmetrics' Media Impact Value® (MIV®) — the industry-standard metric for quantifying the monetary value of media exposure across print, digital, and social — placed Gucci at $91 million for the Milan Fashion Week FW26 season, ranking second behind Prada's $117.9 million.

The total MFW FW26 season generated $638.7 million in MIV across all brands. Gucci's 14.2% share of that total — for a debut collection from a new creative director — represents a significant opening position. Tagwalk independently ranked Gucci second in fashion month overall, citing the star-studded cast as a driver of global visibility.

The Verdict

Demna's Gucci debut generated the highest single-hour mention peak of Milan Fashion Week FW26 and secured the #2 position in both share of voice and Media Impact Value. For a first runway show under a new creative director — at a house that has been navigating a difficult transition — these are strong opening numbers.

The mixed sentiment is expected and arguably healthy: it signals genuine cultural engagement rather than polite indifference. The collection's deliberate sexuality and its references to the Tom Ford era gave the internet something to argue about, which is itself a form of brand heat.

The key question for subsequent seasons: can Demna convert this attention into sustained commercial momentum? The Bamboo 1947 bag update and the immediate post-show retail drop suggest the house is already thinking about the runway-to-retail pipeline. The data will follow.

A transparent, data-driven ranking of the world's most in-demand fashion brands — scored entirely from public, verifiable sources. No black boxes. No platform bias. Just signals.

Q1 2026 Overview

Heritage Reclaims the Throne

The first quarter of 2026 was defined by the enduring dominance of the mega-houses and the dramatic consequences of creative leadership change. Louis Vuitton, Dior, Chanel, and Gucci claimed the top four positions — a consolidation of heritage power that reflects both the resilience of these brands and the limitations of newer entrants to sustain comparable levels of public attention.

We evaluated 31 global fashion houses across three data pillars: social following, web traffic, and search interest.

"The Brand Heat Index exists to separate the two by giving brands, buyers, and industry professionals a clear, unbiased view of where public attention is actually concentrated, not where it's being directed." says Jeanel Alvarado, Editor-in-Chief of Retailboss.

The Q1 2026 findings: heritage houses lead by a significant margin, Louis Vuitton commands a position that most industry indices fail to capture, and the gap between perceived momentum and measurable demand is wider than the prevailing narrative suggests.

Louis Vuitton leads the index with a Heat Score of 91.3, driven by 56 million Instagram followers, 18.1 million monthly web visits, and a search interest ratio that nearly doubles its nearest brand. Dior, Chanel, and Gucci hold the second through fourth positions, confirming the sustained dominance of the major heritage houses. Prada and Hermès round out the top six.

Coach claims the highest web traffic score in the entire index, ranking seventh overall, a signal that consumer engagement extends well beyond the accessible luxury tier. What the data proves is simple: the most talked-about brands are not always the most in-demand.

TIER I — DOMINANT

Heat Score 50+

Key Signals

Louis Vuitton

LVMH · Paris, France · Founded 1854

There is no close second. Louis Vuitton scores a perfect 100 on both the social and search pillars — the only brand in the 31-brand universe to max out two of three metrics — and its web traffic of 18.1 million monthly visits is the highest of any fashion house tracked. These are not vanity metrics. They represent the aggregate of 56 million Instagram followers, 15.9 million TikTok followers, and a search interest that runs 1.85 times higher than the index's own baseline brand.

Q1 2026 was not without turbulence for LVMH's flagship. The group reported first-quarter organic sales growth of just 1% — below analyst expectations — with its Fashion & Leather Goods division down 2%. Yet the public data tells a different story: consumer attention to Louis Vuitton did not waver. The brand's digital footprint remained the largest in luxury fashion by every measurable signal.

LV's position at the top of this index also highlights a structural truth about how fashion heat is measured. Because the house sells exclusively through its own channels — no multi-brand wholesale, no third-party platforms — its web traffic is entirely direct demand. Every one of those 18.1 million monthly visits is a consumer who sought out Louis Vuitton by name.

Key Signals

Dior

LVMH · Paris, France · Founded 1946

Dior is the most balanced brand in the top five — strong across all three pillars without a single dominant spike. Its 44.4 million Instagram followers and 12.5 million TikTok followers place it firmly in the top tier of social reach, while 8.1 million monthly web visits confirm that the audience is active, not passive.

Under Maria Grazia Chiuri's continued creative direction, Dior's Q1 2026 narrative was one of quiet consistency rather than disruption. The house's Spring 2026 campaign — shot in the gardens of the Château de Versailles — generated sustained editorial coverage throughout January and February, maintaining search interest at 0.54 times the index baseline. In a quarter where several houses were defined by their creative transitions, Dior's stability was itself a statement.

Key Signals

Chanel

Chanel S.A. · Paris, France · Founded 1910

Chanel ties Louis Vuitton on the social pillar with a perfect score — 56 million Instagram followers and 8.5 million TikTok followers — making it one of only two brands to achieve a social maximum. What separates it from LV is web traffic: Chanel's 11.5 million monthly visits, while impressive, trail LV's 18.1 million, reflecting the structural difference between a house that sells through its own e-commerce and one that drives consumers to boutiques.

The first quarter of 2026 marked Chanel's continued navigation of the post-Karl Lagerfeld, post-Virginie Viard era under new creative director Matthieu Blazy, who presented his second full collection in January. The critical response was warm — Blazy's instinct for precise, wearable luxury resonated with a market that had grown weary of spectacle. Consumer search interest held steady at 0.54 times the baseline, identical to Dior, suggesting the two houses are operating at near-identical levels of active consumer intent.

Key Signals

Gucci

Kering · Florence, Italy · Founded 1921

February 27, 2026 was the most anticipated date on the fashion calendar. Nearly a year after Demna Gvasalia was announced as Gucci's new creative director, he finally stepped onto the runway. The show, staged in Milan's Palazzo Delle Scintille, was built around a "museum" of Roman statuary scanned from the Uffizi. "My idea was to put Gucci back in the cultural spotlight," Demna told press.

The data suggests he succeeded — at least in generating attention. Demand for Gucci rose 12% in the 24 hours following the show, and the brand's Q1 web traffic of 8.4 million monthly visits matched Dior's. With 49.2 million Instagram followers and 10.2 million TikTok followers, Gucci's social footprint is the third-largest in the index.

The commercial reality was more complicated: Kering reported Gucci sales down 8% in Q1 2026. But brand heat and brand revenue are different signals, and Q1 2026 was the quarter in which Gucci's heat — driven by Demna's debut — clearly outpaced its commercial performance.

Key Signals

Prada

Prada Group · Milan, Italy · Founded 1913

Prada is the only brand in the index to score above 40 on all three pillars simultaneously — a consistency that reflects the house's remarkable decade-long run of critical and commercial relevance under Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons. The Prada Group reported 3% organic sales growth in Q1 2026, making it one of the few luxury groups to post positive numbers in a challenging quarter.

With 32.2 million Instagram followers, 7.0 million TikTok followers, and 7.8 million monthly web visits, Prada's data profile is the most evenly distributed of any brand in the top five. It does not dominate any single metric, but it is competitive across all of them — a reflection of a brand that has successfully cultivated relevance across demographics without compromising its intellectual identity.

TIER II — STRONG

Heat Score 30–49

Key Signals

Hermès

Hermès International · Paris, France · Founded 1837

Hermès presents the most fascinating data anomaly in the index. With only 12.9 million Instagram followers — modest by mega-house standards — it generates 1.85 times Gucci's search interest and 8.8 million monthly web visits. The search-to-follower ratio is the highest of any brand in the 31-brand universe, suggesting a consumer base that is actively seeking the brand rather than passively following it.

This is the Hermès paradox: a house that has deliberately resisted the social media arms race — no celebrity collaborations, no viral stunts, no TikTok-first strategy — yet commands more active consumer intent than brands with four times its follower count. The Birkin waitlist is not a social media phenomenon. It is a demand signal that shows up in search data, in web traffic, and in the secondary market.

Q1 2026 was a difficult quarter for Hermès at the corporate level: shares fell as much as 23% year-to-date amid geopolitical tensions and slower Chinese demand. But the public data — the consumer-facing signals — showed no equivalent deterioration. Brand heat and stock price are different things.

Key Signals

Coach

Tapestry Inc. · New York, USA · Founded 1941

Coach scores a perfect 100 on the web traffic pillar — the only brand in the index to max out this metric — with 18.5 million monthly website visits, the highest raw traffic figure of all 31 brands evaluated. This is a genuine signal of consumer demand: Coach's e-commerce and direct-to-consumer model drives an enormous volume of active website engagement, reflecting strong purchase intent from its core American consumer base.

The brand's social and search scores are more modest: 8.1 million Instagram followers and a search score adjusted downward to account for the significant volume of non-fashion "coach" queries (sports coaching, life coaching, school bus). The adjusted search figure is conservative — the unadjusted score would place Coach considerably higher. This is one of the index's most transparent data quality flags.

Key Signals

Versace

Capri Holdings · Milan, Italy · Founded 1978

Versace is the index's most dramatic momentum story. A +47.9% month-on-month web traffic surge in Q1 2026 — the largest of any brand tracked — propelled the house from a mid-table position into the top ten. The driver: Dario Vitale, the Milanese designer appointed as creative director following Donatella Versace's transition to a brand ambassador role, presented his debut collection to significant critical and commercial attention.

With 29.3 million Instagram followers and 4.2 million TikTok followers, Versace's social footprint is the fifth-largest in the index — a legacy of Donatella's decades of celebrity cultivation and the house's innate understanding of spectacle. The question for the next two quarters is whether Vitale can convert the attention spike into sustained demand.

Key Signals

Ralph Lauren

Ralph Lauren Corp. · New York, USA · Founded 1967

Ralph Lauren is the American heritage story that the data consistently validates. With 8.1 million monthly web visits — matching Dior — and a stable social presence of 16.2 million Instagram followers, the brand demonstrates that its cultural relevance extends well beyond its core demographic.

Q1 2026 saw Ralph Lauren benefit from the broader "quiet luxury" and "old money aesthetic" trend cycles that continued to drive consumer interest in heritage American brands. The house's consistent web traffic, combined with its strong TikTok presence of 3.5 million followers, suggests a brand successfully navigating the generational transition without abandoning its identity.

Key Signals

Balenciaga

Kering · Paris, France · Founded 1919

Balenciaga enters the index in the post-Demna era — the Georgian designer's departure for Gucci left the house without a creative director for the first quarter, creating a strategic vacuum that is visible in the data. A -4.2% month-on-month web traffic decline and a web score of 22.2 reflect a house in transition.

Yet the social numbers tell a more resilient story: 24.4 million Instagram followers and 5.8 million TikTok followers — the latter the fourth-highest in the index — suggest that the brand's cultural capital, built over a decade of Demna's provocations, has not evaporated. The question is whether Kering can find a successor who can channel that capital into new creative energy.

TIER III — ESTABLISHED

Heat Score 20–29

Key Signals

Burberry

Burberry Group plc · London, UK · Founded 1856

Burberry's Q1 2026 data reflects a house in the early stages of a genuine turnaround. Under Daniel Lee, who has now had three full years to reshape the brand's identity, the trench coat — Burberry's most iconic product — has been repositioned as a luxury statement rather than a heritage commodity. The +2.1% month-on-month web traffic growth, while modest, represents a reversal of the declining trend that characterized the brand's 2024 performance.

With 16.2 million Instagram followers and 5.1 million monthly web visits, Burberry sits at the lower end of the Tier II range — a reflection of the brand's ongoing repositioning from accessible luxury to true luxury. The data suggests the repositioning is working, but the full effect will take several more quarters to manifest in the index's metrics.

Key Signals

Off-White

Farfetch/LVMH · Milan, Italy · Founded 2012

Off-White's presence in the index reflects the enduring cultural capital of Virgil Abloh's creation rather than the brand's current commercial trajectory. With 9.0 million Instagram followers and a search interest that remains above the index's lower threshold, the brand continues to generate consumer attention — but the gap between attention and conversion is widening.

Revenue declined an estimated 20–50% in 2025, and the brand's web traffic of 772,000 monthly visits is the lowest of any brand in the top 15. The creative direction under Ibrahim Kamara has struggled to generate the same cultural urgency that defined the Abloh era. Off-White's position in this index is, in part, a reflection of the lag between cultural perception and data reality.

Key Signals

Miu Miu

Prada Group · Milan, Italy · Founded 1992

Miu Miu's position at #13 in the data-driven index — compared to #4 in platform-based rankings — is the clearest illustration of the gap between editorial perception and public data. The brand's 2.2 million monthly web visits are the lowest of any brand in the top 15, and its Instagram following of 8.1 million is modest relative to its cultural profile.

The discrepancy is likely explained by Miu Miu's strength on fashion-specific platforms and in editorial coverage — signals that are not captured by general web traffic or broad social metrics. The brand's micro-skirt moment and its status as the critical darling of the past three seasons are real phenomena; they simply do not show up in the same way in publicly available data as they do in platform-specific demand signals.

Key Signals

Jacquemus

Independent · Paris, France · Founded 2009

Jacquemus is the independent luxury success story of the past decade — a brand built almost entirely on Simon Porte Jacquemus's personal Instagram presence and a series of spectacular show locations, from the lavender fields of Provence to the salt flats of the Camargue. With 12.1 million Instagram followers and 2.5 million TikTok followers, the brand punches significantly above its revenue weight in social terms.

The 2.5 million monthly web visits reflect a brand that has successfully converted social attention into commercial traffic, even if the absolute numbers remain modest relative to the mega-houses. Q1 2026 saw Jacquemus continue its global expansion, with new store openings in New York and Tokyo reinforcing the brand's ambition to move from cult status to genuine luxury scale.

Key Signals

Valentino

Mayhoola · Rome, Italy · Founded 1960

Valentino's score is driven almost entirely by its social pillar — 18.9 million Instagram followers give it the sixth-largest social following in the index — while its web traffic of 1.4 million monthly visits is the second-lowest in the top 15. This social-to-web gap suggests a brand with strong aspirational appeal but limited direct e-commerce conversion.

Under Alessandro Michele, who joined from Gucci in late 2023, Valentino has been in a period of creative reinvention. Michele's maximalist aesthetic — which defined Gucci's cultural moment from 2015 to 2022 — is being reinterpreted for a Roman house with different heritage codes. Q1 2026 was the first full quarter in which Michele's vision was fully visible in stores, and the social data suggests consumer curiosity remains high.

TIER IV — CONTENDERS

Heat Score 15–21

Key Signals

Bottega Veneta

Kering · Vicenza, Italy · Founded 1966

Bottega Veneta occupies the sixteenth position in the Q1 2026 Brand Heat Index. Its intrecciato leather craft and Matthieu Blazy-era design legacy have sustained a loyal, high-value consumer base that operates largely outside conventional digital channels.

The brand's deliberately minimal digital presence — 4.0 million Instagram followers, no TikTok strategy — is a conscious brand decision. Bottega Veneta's consumer is not primarily a social media consumer. The brand's 3.1 million monthly web visits and strong secondary market performance suggest a customer base that does not require social amplification to maintain its purchasing behavior.

Key Signals

Saint Laurent

Kering · Paris, France · Founded 1961

Saint Laurent's #17 position in this index — compared to #2 in platform-based rankings — is the most significant divergence in the entire dataset, and it warrants direct explanation. The brand's 3.4 million monthly web visits, 8.1 million Instagram followers, and 0.27× search ratio simply do not support a top-two ranking by any publicly verifiable metric.

This does not mean Saint Laurent is not a culturally significant brand. It means that its significance is concentrated in channels — editorial coverage, wholesale platform demand, celebrity dressing — that are not captured by the three pillars of this index. The gap between Saint Laurent's platform ranking and its public data ranking is the clearest argument for why transparent, multi-source indexing matters.

Key Signals

Loewe

LVMH · Madrid, Spain · Founded 1846

Loewe under Jonathan Anderson has been one of the critical success stories of the past five years — a Spanish leather goods house transformed into one of the most intellectually rigorous and culturally engaged brands in luxury. The brand's Craft Prize, its collaborations with artists and artisans, and Anderson's instinct for cultural relevance have generated enormous editorial goodwill.

The public data, however, reflects a brand that remains relatively niche in terms of raw consumer reach: 2.5 million monthly web visits and 8.1 million Instagram followers are modest by mega-house standards. Anderson's departure for Dior — announced in late 2025 — will be the defining event for Loewe in 2026, and its impact on the brand's data profile will be closely watched.

Key Signals

Celine

LVMH · Paris, France · Founded 1945

Celine's search data requires a significant adjustment: a substantial portion of "Celine" search queries relate to Celine Dion, the Canadian singer, rather than the French fashion house. The adjusted search score is conservative and may understate the brand's true fashion-specific search interest.

Under Hedi Slimane, Celine has maintained a deliberately minimal digital presence — 4.0 million Instagram followers and 0.5 million TikTok followers reflect a brand that does not compete for social reach. The 4.1 million monthly web visits suggest a loyal consumer base that seeks the brand out directly, consistent with Slimane's vision of Celine as a house for consumers who do not need to be told what to want.

Key Signals

Fendi

LVMH · Rome, Italy · Founded 1925

Fendi closes the index with a -9.9% month-on-month web traffic decline — the second-largest negative momentum figure in the top 20. The Roman house, under Kim Jones's creative direction, has struggled to generate the same level of cultural conversation as its LVMH stablemates Dior and Louis Vuitton.

With 8.1 million Instagram followers and 3.1 million monthly web visits, Fendi's data profile is consistent with a brand that maintains strong heritage recognition but has not yet found the creative catalyst that would elevate it to the next tier. The Baguette bag remains a cultural touchstone, and the brand's Roman identity — reinforced by its Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana headquarters — provides a distinctive positioning that the data does not yet fully reflect.

Q1 2026 Macro Trends

Six Themes Defining the Quarter

The Creative Director Effect

New creative appointments generated the most dramatic web traffic swings of the quarter. Versace's +47.9% MoM surge following Dario Vitale's debut and Gucci's +12% demand spike after Demna's first show confirm that a single runway moment can move the needle on public data signals within 24 hours.

Heat ≠ Revenue

The most striking divergence in Q1 2026 is between brand heat and brand revenue. Gucci scored #4 in this index while reporting -8% sales. Louis Vuitton topped the index while LVMH's Fashion & Leather Goods division declined 2%. Consumer attention and consumer spending are increasingly decoupled.

The Search Premium

Hermès generates 1.85× Gucci's search interest with only 12.9M Instagram followers versus Gucci's 49.2M. The search-to-follower ratio is the most revealing metric in the index: it separates brands that are followed from brands that are actively sought. Hermès is the clearest example of the latter.

DTC Dominates

Brands with direct-to-consumer e-commerce channels average 13.0M monthly web visits versus 7.6M for brands reliant on multi-brand wholesale. The 65% gap reflects a structural advantage: every DTC visit is a direct demand signal, while wholesale traffic is fragmented across third-party platforms.

TikTok as Tier Separator

Average TikTok followers for Tier I brands: 11.2M. Tier II: 3.5M. Tiers III and IV: below 2.5M. The 3.5M threshold is emerging as the dividing line between brands with genuine Gen Z cultural penetration and those that remain primarily Millennial or older in their digital reach.

The Quiet Luxury Ceiling

Brands associated with the 'quiet luxury' aesthetic — Saint Laurent, The Row, Celine, Bottega Veneta — consistently score lower in this index than their editorial profiles suggest. The exception is Hermès, whose search premium saves it. Public data does not capture the word-of-mouth and in-store dynamics that drive quiet luxury demand.
